question_en: The advantage of automatic stabilizers over discretionary fiscal policy is that they most likely:
option_a: affect real GDP growth rates more rapidly.
option_b: have a greater impact on GDP per unit of fiscal expenditure.
option_c: can be more precisely calibrated to achieve the desired impact.
explanation_en: Discretionary fiscal policies (ie, government spending and taxes) require specific actions (eg, legislation) to be implemented. However, various lags impede the effectiveness of discretionary fiscal policy. In contrast, automatic stabilizers are programs already in place that are triggered by changes in economic activity, so they are not subject to these lags. Automatic stabilizers steady the economy by their countercyclical nature. Examples of automatic stabilizers include: Unemployment benefits: Unemployment increases as economies weaken, so government spending on these programs increases. The reverse occurs when economies strengthen. Progressive income tax: Incomes rise as economies strengthen, placing more workers in higher tax brackets, resulting in less spending relative to income. The reverse occurs when economies weaken. (Choice B) The economic impact on GDP per unit of fiscal expenditure is not determined by whether it results from automatic stabilizers or discretionary policy. The impact depends on the timing and the change in spending or tax revenues. (Choice C) Discretionary fiscal policy can achieve very specific changes in government spending or tax rates. The impact of automatic stabilizers, however, cannot be precisely quantified because spending and tax revenue changes depend on the level of economic activity, which cannot be accurately predicted.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\2. Economics\2.03 Fiscal Policy - Answers.pdf
question_en: Which of the following is the most appropriate argument in support of larger government budget deficits during a recession, despite high levels of government debt relative to GDP?
option_a: Higher taxes can be imposed to pay the debt.
option_b: Increased debt can result in the utilization of idle resources.
option_c: Governments can borrow at lower rates than businesses or consumers.
explanation_en: Government debt reflects a government's cumulative budget deficits (ie, shortfalls of revenues versus expenditures). Economists disagree about the significance of high levels of government debt relative to GDP. Those who favor increasing already high levels of debt argue that budget deficits may generate economic growth if there are underutilized resources. In recessions, the unemployment rate is relatively high and capacity utilization is low. Increases in government debt resulting from tax cuts or spending increases do not necessarily divert resources from productive uses. Therefore, a budget deficit can result in higher levels of employment and GDP growth. (Choice A) Raising taxes to repay debt may be a disincentive to economic activity. Higher tax rates may reduce the incentive to work and invest, leading to lower growth in the long run. (Choice C) Governments can usually borrow at lower rates than businesses or consumers. However, this may crowd out other borrowers and lead to higher interest rates on the smaller pool of capital for private borrowers.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\2. Economics\2.03 Fiscal Policy - Answers.pdf
question_en: An economist reads the following statement in a research article: "If a country's national debt is financed by borrowing, the size of its national debt relative to GDP may not matter, in the long run." This statement is most likely supported if:
option_b: most of the debt is owed to the country's own citizens.
option_c: the debt reduces incentives for consumers to increase savings.
explanation_en: Economists debate whether the size of a country's national debt relative to GDP matters. If the debt grows too large relative to GDP, it may cast doubt on the country's ability to pay its debts in the future (ie, solvency). Interest payments on the debt may burden the current budget. A large existing national debt may also hinder efforts at expansionary fiscal policy, which typically enlarges public debt. One factor that eases these concerns is if most of a country's debt is owed internally to fellow citizens, as is currently the case in Japan and South Korea, for example. (Choice A) Too much government borrowing may discourage or "crowd out" private borrowing and investment, both by diverting capital from the private sector and by creating greater demand for capital that pushes up interest rates. This scenario would support the argument that the size of the national debt relative to GDP does matter. (Choice C) Concerns about the size of government debt relative to GDP would be countered by increased consumer saving rates, particularly if consumers increased saving rates in anticipation of supporting the higher debt. Adding, not reducing, incentives for consumers to save would be a condition that would support this statement.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\2. Economics\2.04 Monetary Policy - Answers.pdf
question_en: Open market purchases of government securities by a central bank are most likely:
option_b: expansionary.
option_c: contractionary.
explanation_en: Monetary policy tools Tool Description Expansionary Contractionary Open market operations Trade securities (usually government securities) Buy securities Sell securities Policy interest rate Set interest rate used to signal markets Lower Raise Reserve requirements Set percentage of bank deposits held in reserves Decrease Increase Open market operations (ie, buying or selling government securities) is the most frequently used monetary policy tool for most major central banks. Central bank purchases of securities are an expansionary policy. Central banks usually purchase securities from commercial banks or designated market makers. The immediate impact is an increase in bank reserves. Banks employ the additional reserves by making loans or investments, which results in an expansion of the money supply. As the money supply increases, the cost of borrowing (ie, interest rates) tends to fall. Lower interest rates stimulate borrowing by consumers to buy houses, cars, appliances, and other major items. Lower rates also encourage businesses to invest because profit margins will be higher due to lowered interest expenses. Additionally, some projects not viable at the previous borrowing cost may now be profitable.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\2. Economics\2.04 Monetary Policy - Answers.pdf
question_en: In an economy that operates under an exchange rate targeting policy, which of the following conditions is most likely?
option_a: The central bank is required to maintain a fixed policy interest rate.
option_b: Monetary policy can focus on internal rather than external considerations.
option_c: Target country inflation (deflation) is imported regardless of the effect on the domestic
explanation_en: Monetary policy targets Stated Long-run Country policy target economic goal characteristics Fixed rate or Price stability leading to better long- Inflation range for specified run performance price index Larger, Optimize across more developed economies Interest multiple goals Target adjusted over business cycle rates (employment, GDP growth) Smaller, Exchange Fixed rate or range versus target Stability versus economies of major less developed rate currency trading partners with significant import/export sectors The goal of monetary policy is to optimize economic welfare, although central banks are given a variety of policy targets intended to attain that goal. Central banks may have: One policy target (ie, single mandate) that guides all policy actions: A specific inflation target (eg, 2%) or a specified range An exchange rate target, which is a fixed level or band of values versus a major currency (eg, EUR) Multiple policy targets that seek an optimal balance among potentially conflicting goals: High employment GDP growth Stable prices Stable exchange rate When a country uses exchange rate targeting, its policies are designed to maintain an exchange rate target (or range) with another currency, usually from a larger and/or more stable economy. As a result, if the target currency's economy experiences inflation or deflation, so does the economy that targets it. In this situation, since all policy actions must be aimed at maintaining the targeted currency exchange value, the targeting economy gives up monetary policy independence. This may adversely affect both the targeting economy and its ability to address any adverse effects. For example, exchange rate targeting may keep a central bank from exercising independent monetary policies based solely on domestic conditions, such as maintaining a fixed policy interest rate or adjusting monetary policy (Choices A and B).

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\2. Economics\2.04 Monetary Policy - Answers.pdf
question_en: A developing economy has a target exchange rate for its currency. The inflation rate in the developing economy drops below the inflation rate in the target currency. Central bank action to defend the target exchange rate is most likely to result in a decrease in the developing economy's:
option_b: short-term interest rates.
option_c: balance of payments surplus.
explanation_en: A country forgoes monetary policy independence if it establishes a target exchange value for its currency. Monetary policy cannot pursue goals related to GDP growth, unemployment, or inflation. Policy actions are driven by the demands of maintaining the announced exchange rate target. The domestic economy must adapt to the policy of the target currency country. This often results in increased volatility of the domestic money supply and interest rates. Domestic inflation rates below target currency inflation rates put upward pressure on the exchange value of the developing economy's currency. To offset the currency market pressure and maintain the target exchange rate, the central bank must sell its currency and buy the target currency. Sales of the developing economy currency will expand the domestic money supply and decrease interest rates. (Choice A) The central bank needs to sell the domestic currency to maintain the target exchange rate. This would increase the domestic money supply. (Choice C) The balance of payments must always net to zero, so there can be neither a surplus nor a deficit.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\2. Economics\2.04 Monetary Policy - Answers.pdf
question_en: Which of the following is most likely a role of a central bank?
option_b: Sets long-term interest rates
option_c: Acts as lender of last resort to banks
explanation_en: Typical roles of a central bank Lender of last resort Supplier of currency Responsible for monetary policy Serves as the government's and banker's bank Oversees the banking system Regulates the payments system Manages foreign exchange and gold reserves Central banks are a key component of a modern, financially connected world. The roles and responsibilities of central banks can be broadly split into banking and monetary functions. Banking responsibilities include overseeing and regulating the banking and payment processing system. A central bank also functions as the government's and bankers' bank, providing funds and liquidity when needed. As such, central banks are ultimately the lender of last resort to banks, when other sources of capital are unavailable. Monetary responsibilities include money creation and, to a certain extent, overseeing the value of the currency. This leads directly to the role of conducting monetary policy and managing a country's foreign exchange and gold reserves. (Choice A) Central banks do not issue debt; this is usually a treasury function. (Choice B) Central banks set short-term interest rates through monetary policy, not long-term rates.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\2. Economics\2.04 Monetary Policy - Answers.pdf
question_en: Which of the following best characterizes the approach most central banks take regarding inflation?
option_b: Maintain targeted inflation rates
option_c: Accept market-determined inflation rates
explanation_en: Periods of high inflation usually coincide with poor economic growth and greater inflation uncertainty. Unexpected inflation carries great economic costs (eg, low GDP growth). Consequently, price stability is a primary goal for most central banks. As a means of attaining that goal, target inflation rates consistent with price stability are established. Quality improvements complicate measuring changes in the cost of living. Innovation leads to the creation of more useful (ie, valuable) products over time. Some amount of price level increase reflects the higher quality goods, not an erosion in the purchasing power of money. Therefore, price stability is not defined as a 0% inflation rate. Instead, it is defined as a low and stable inflation rate (one generally consistent with product enhancements). In some countries the inflation target is set by the government. In other countries the central banks set the inflation target independently of the government; such central banks are said to be target independent. Central banks' performance is assessed in part by monitoring their effectiveness at keeping inflation within the target range. (Choice A) Central banks do not attempt to achieve the lowest possible inflation rates. Very low inflation (eg, <1%) or negative inflation (ie, deflation) is believed to inhibit an economy from fully achieving its potential GDP. (Choice C) Central banks believe the goal of price stability is too important to allow inflation to result from the unconstrained interplay of market forces. All major central banks have inflation targets or target ranges for achieving price stability.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\2. Economics\2.04 Monetary Policy - Answers.pdf
question_en: Which of the following best describes a contractionary fiscal policy?
option_a: A decrease in the government budget surplus
option_b: A reduction in export subsidies to manufacturers
option_c: An expansion of eligibility for unemployment benefits
explanation_en: Contractionary fiscal policies are designed to constrain economic growth. Contractionary policies are usually not intended to literally contract (ie, shrink) the size of an economy but to prevent an economy from growing too rapidly. Excessive growth relative to an economy's sustainable growth rate is a possible cause of inflation. Increased taxation and reduced spending are contractionary fiscal policies. Export subsidies are payments made by the government to domestic businesses designed to increase exports. A reduction in export subsidies reduces government payments to the exporters. The direct contractionary impact is lower revenue for the manufacturers. The result is fewer purchases of materials and cutbacks on employee hours. The effects filter through the economy as other impacted suppliers and employees reduce their spending accordingly. (Choice A) Other things constant, decreases in government budget surpluses are expansionary. Reductions in government budget surpluses result from increases in spending or reductions in taxes (or both). Since both of those government actions are expansionary, smaller surpluses lead to increases in GDP. (Choice C) Increasing government transfer payments is an expansionary policy. Expanded eligibility for unemployment benefits generally results in more total money being paid to beneficiaries. The consequence is greater consumption spending and higher GDP.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\2. Economics\2.04 Monetary Policy - Answers.pdf
question_en: If a central bank wants to increase the money supply, the most appropriate action it can take is to:
option_b: reduce the reserve requirements.
option_c: sell government bonds to commercial banks.
explanation_en: Monetary policy tools Tool Description Expansionary Contractionary Open market operations Trade securities (usually government securities) Buy securities Sell securities Policy interest rate Set interest rate used to signal markets Lower Raise Reserve requirements Set percentage of bank deposits held in reserves Decrease Increase In a system of fractional reserve banking, reserve requirements are one policy tool used by central banks to control the money supply and, in turn, spending and economic growth. Reserve requirements set the minimum percentage of commercial banks' deposit liabilities that must be held as reserves; banks make loans with the excess deposits. Lowering the reserve requirements for commercial banks allows those banks to lend more money. In theory, this should increase the money supply since additional money lent by banks can be deposited and lent multiple times. Thus, there is an inverse relationship between reserve requirements and the amount of money created, as reflected by the money multiplier. All else being equal, the smaller (larger) the reserve requirement is: the larger (smaller) the money multiplier, and the more (less) money is created by fractional reserve banking, and the greater (smaller) the money supply. (Choice A) Increasing the policy rate makes taking out short-term loans from the central bank more expensive for commercial banks. This typically causes commercial banks to increase their own lending rates, which lowers demand for loans and reduces the money supply. (Choice C) Selling securities to commercial banks reduces the commercial banks' reserves and typically makes them less willing and/or able to make loans, which reduces the money supply.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\2. Economics\2.04 Monetary Policy - Answers.pdf
question_en: Which of the following is least likely a quality of an effective central bank?
option_b: Independence
option_c: Creditworthiness
explanation_en: The qualities of effective central banks are independence, credibility, and transparency. Since central banks do not issue debt securities, the ability to repay debt in a timely fashion (ie, creditworthiness) is not a factor in assessing their effectiveness. Major central banks have large amounts of liabilities outstanding; however, the liabilities are either physical currency issued by the central bank or deposits (by other financial institutions) held at the central bank. As such, central bank liabilities have no stated maturity and do not need to be retired. Furthermore, most central banks face no legal limits on the amount of money they can create. This means any requests for withdrawals can be honored; therefore, creditworthiness is not a factor for central banks. (Choices A and B) Central banks should have independence since they must be able to act considering only the long-term economic consequences, not the short-term political consequences, of their actions. Independence is supported by transparency in setting policy objectives and actions.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\2. Economics\2.04 Monetary Policy - Answers.pdf
question_en: An increase in which of the following would most appropriately be considered expansionary fiscal policy?
option_a: New excise taxes on vehicle motor fuel
option_b: Infrastructure spending on highways and bridges
option_c: Reducing budget deficits by raising corporate income taxes
explanation_en: Increases in government spending cause an increase in GDP. More infrastructure spending causes the aggregate demand to increase. Consequently, an increase in government spending is an expansionary fiscal policy. The immediate impact of increased spending on highways and bridges is the additional sales revenue for the firms that supply the materials and machinery used in the construction projects. The firms involved in the construction—and their equipment and materials suppliers—will hire additional workers. As a result, aggregate demand is further stimulated by the increased income that workers spend on consumption. (Choice A) A tax on vehicle fuel raises consumers' costs. This puts downward pressure on GDP and is therefore a contractionary policy. (Choice C) Raising corporate income taxes reduces investments and hiring. This is a contractionary policy, not an expansionary policy.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\2. Economics\2.04 Monetary Policy - Answers.pdf
question_en: Which of the following monetary policy actions is most likely expansionary?
option_a: Selling government securities through open market operations
option_b: Lowering the policy rate to a level below the neutral interest rate
option_c: Raising reserve requirements to reduce the amount of excess reserves
explanation_en: Monetary policy tools Tool Description Expansionary Contractionary Open market operations Trade securities (usually government securities) Buy securities Sell securities Policy interest rate Set interest rate used to signal markets Lower Raise Reserve requirements Set percentage of bank deposits held in reserves Decrease Increase Expansionary monetary policies encourage more rapid growth of GDP by stimulating economic activity, including business and consumer investment and consumption. Since businesses borrow to invest in additional plant and equipment and consumers borrow to increase purchases of goods and services, policies that stimulate lending and borrowing are expansionary. A policy rate (ie, official interest rate or official policy rate) is the interest rate a central bank charges when it lends money to commercial banks. Setting the policy rate below a neutral rate of interest means the central bank is attempting to increase the real GDP growth rate by: reducing the cost of borrowing from the central bank, which encourages commercial banks to use additional reserves to make loans, increasing the supply of available credit; and lowering borrowing rates generally since commercial bank base lending rates are often tied to the policy rate, stimulating demand for credit. Since this policy leads to increased lending and borrowing and should stimulate economic growth, it is expansionary. (Choice A) When central banks sell government securities, they reduce bank reserves since commercial banks pay for the securities using reserves. This discourages lending and borrowing and slows GDP growth; therefore, it is a contractionary monetary policy. (Choice C) Raising the reserve requirement to reduce excess reserves inhibits commercial banks' ability to make loans; therefore, it is not an expansionary policy.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\2. Economics\2.04 Monetary Policy - Answers.pdf
question_en: If the inflation rate is expected to rise above a central bank's inflation target, that central bank's most appropriate action would be to:
option_a: increase the policy rate above the neutral rate.
option_b: buy government bonds from commercial banks.
option_c: lower the reserve requirement for commercial banks.
explanation_en: Monetary policy tools Tool Description Expansionary Contractionary Open market operations Trade securities (usually government securities) Buy securities Sell securities Policy interest rate Set interest rate used to signal markets Lower Raise Reserve requirements Set percentage of bank deposits held in reserves Decrease Increase Central banks have different primary policy objectives, but one common goal is price stability. Central banks attempt to achieve this stability by influencing money supply levels with one or more monetary policy tools. When a central bank expects inflation to rise above the target, it would most appropriately seek to curb inflation by implementing a contractionary monetary policy. To accomplish this, the central bank can target an increase in commercial banks' lending rates by increasing its policy rate above the neutral rate. Commercial banks tend to base their lending rates on the policy rate plus a spread. Therefore, a higher policy rate would cause those banks to either raise their lending rates or accept lower margins, thus discouraging lending and borrowing. Less supply and demand for business and consumer loans would slow capital expenditures and consumption. In theory, these effects should lower inflationary pressures. (Choice B) Buying government bonds from commercial banks is an expansionary monetary policy that gives those banks more excess reserves to lend. This policy would be inappropriate if the goal is to reduce inflationary pressures. (Choice C) Lowering the reserve requirement for commercial banks encourages those banks to lend more money. This expansionary monetary policy would be inappropriate if the goal is to reduce inflationary pressures.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\2. Economics\2.04 Monetary Policy - Answers.pdf
question_en: When the central bank sells securities to banks via open market operations, which of the following is the most likely result?
option_b: A decrease in base lending rates
option_c: A decrease in banks' capacity to lend
explanation_en: Monetary policy tools Tool Description Expansionary Contractionary Open market operations Trade securities (usually government securities) Buy securities Sell securities Policy interest rate Set interest rate used to signal markets Lower Raise Reserve requirements Set percentage of bank deposits held in reserves Decrease Increase Central banks use monetary policy tools to manage the money supply and achieve price stability. When the economy is growing too fast and inflation is high, central banks will enact contractionary policies to reduce the money supply to moderate growth and inflation. When the economy is slow and inflation is low, central banks will enact expansionary policies to increase the money supply to accelerate growth and inflation. Open market operations involve the central bank buying (selling) securities from (to) banks or market makers. Selling securities to banks is a contractionary tactic. Bank reserves are reduced when commercial banks buy securities as the central banks sells securities (Choice A); in effect, the central bank has taken money out of circulation. Since bank reserves are lower, banks are less willing and/or able to extend loans, reducing the money supply. (Choice B) Base lending rates used by banks are directly tied to the central bank policy rate and not related to open market operations.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\2. Economics\2.04 Monetary Policy - Answers.pdf
question_en: Most central banks with an inflation-targeting policy aim for an inflation rate of about 2%. Which of the following best describes a reason why this level has become the prevailing standard?
option_a: A lower rate would risk deflation
option_b: To adhere to a neutral policy rate
option_c: To keep the country's borrowing costs low
explanation_en: Features of successful central bank inflation-targeting policy Central bank independence and transparency Policy decisions based on a wide range of financial and economic considerations An inflation target high enough to avoid deflation but low enough to achieve price stability Inflation targeting is the most widely implemented central bank monetary policy framework used to achieve price stability. Broadly speaking, monetary policy is a blunt tool that influences the economy and inflation to varying degrees and with lagged effects. With inflation targeting, the central bank's goal is to maintain an inflation rate low enough to avoid destabilizing inflation yet high enough to avoid the risk of deflation. Since it is not possible to precisely calibrate monetary policy to achieve an ideal inflation rate—consistently positive and just above zero—the prevailing preference among central banks has settled around a 2% inflation target as the optimum policy level. (Choice B) The neutral policy rate is the monetary policy rate that maintains the existing state of economic growth. The neutral policy rate equals the economy's real trend rate of growth plus long-run inflation rate expectations. (Choice C) Keeping the government's interest costs low is not a stated objective of monetary policy for any of the world's major central banks.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\2. Economics\2.04 Monetary Policy - Answers.pdf
question_en: If a monetary system has a fractional reserve banking system and the central bank changes the reserve requirement from 10% to 12%, it is most likely that:
option_b: money supply growth increases.
option_c: interest rates on bank deposits decrease.
explanation_en: With a fractional reserve banking system, banks keep only a portion (ie, fraction) of deposits as reserves and make loans with the excess. The minimum reserve requirement is most often set by the central bank and is one of three primary tools of monetary policy. In theory, the smaller (larger) the reserve requirement, the more (less) excess there is to be lent out and circulated in the economy, increasing (decreasing) the money supply and stimulating (contracting) spending and economic growth. The money multiplier is a measure of the inverse effect of the reserve requirement on the money supply, defined as 1 ÷ reserve requirement. For example, a reserve requirement of 10% results in a money multiplier of 10. Each deposit in excess of the reserve requirement is multiplied as it is loaned and deposited multiple times, each time as a fraction of the initial deposit. Therefore, as the reserve requirement increases (decreases), the money multiplier decreases (increases), resulting in slower (faster) money supply growth (Choice B). (Choice C) Interest rates on bank deposits are primarily a function of the central bank's policy rate, not the reserve requirement.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\2. Economics\2.04 Monetary Policy - Answers.pdf
question_en: When the commercial banking system holds significant excess reserves, which of the following central bank actions is most likely to affect commercial banks' base lending rates?
option_b: Changing the reserve requirement
option_c: Buying or selling securities in the open market
explanation_en: Monetary policy tools Tool Description Expansionary Contractionary Open market operations Trade securities (usually government securities) Buy securities Sell securities Policy interest rate Set interest rate used to signal markets Lower Raise Reserve requirements Set percentage of bank deposits held in reserves Decrease Increase A policy rate (or official interest rate or official policy rate) is the rate at which a central bank lends to commercial banks. Policy rates are adjusted to influence interest rates throughout the economy and affect economic activity. Since the policy rate is the cost of obtaining reserves from the central bank, commercial banks often tie base lending rates to the central bank policy rate. Therefore, commercial banks usually increase their base lending rate when a central bank increases its policy rate. Base lending rates are reference rates for setting loan interest rates for different types of clients (eg, large corporations: Base lending rate + 0.50%; privately held small businesses: Base lending rate + 3.00%). Since changing reserve requirements and buying or selling securities affects reserves, such policy actions by central banks are less likely to impact base lending rates when there are already significant excess reserves and therefore ample capacity to make loans and expand the money supply (Choices B and C).

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\2. Economics\2.04 Monetary Policy - Answers.pdf
question_en: A demand curve for money is depicted in the graph below: Which of the following best explains the shape of the curve between M and M ?
option_b: Policy rate of zero
option_c: Neutral rate of interest
explanation_en: Monetary policy tools Tool Description Expansionary Contractionary Open market operations Trade securities (usually government securities) Buy securities Sell securities Policy interest rate Set interest rate used to signal markets Lower Raise Reserve requirements Set percentage of bank deposits held in reserves Decrease Increase Quantitative easing (QE) is operationally equivalent to buying securities through open market operations. QE is pursued after other expansionary policies (eg, decreasing interest rates) have failed to return the economy to its potential growth rate. QE is intended to prevent a recession from becoming a depression. The differences between open market operations and QE are the scale of the purchases, the types of securities purchased, and the sellers. In the aftermath of the 2008 financial crisis, QE purchases were of unprecedented magnitude (multiple trillions of USD or similar values of EUR, GBP, and JPY). Furthermore, whereas open market operations normally dealt in short-term government securities, QE purchases were often long-term government securities and securities of other issuers (eg, corporate bonds). Also, many sellers were not from the usual group of banks and market makers. (Choices A and C) Neither changing the reserve requirement nor adjusting the policy rate (also called the official interest rate or official policy rate) requires central banks to trade securities; therefore, neither is operationally similar to QE.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\2. Economics\2.04 Monetary Policy - Answers.pdf
question_en: Quantitative easing is operationally similar to which monetary policy tool?
option_b: Conducting open market operations
option_c: Increasing or decreasing the policy rate
explanation_en: Monetary policy actions are typically used to affect one or more of the following domestic economic variables: GDP growth, inflation, interest rates, and/or currency value. Monetary policies are either: expansionary, which are typically used to increase economic growth when it is below potential GDP or when the economy is in recession, or contractionary, which are typically used to reduce inflation expectations and often accompanied by policies that reduce expected GDP growth rates. A policy of central bank open market purchases of securities is an expansionary policy. Such purchases increase commercial bank reserves, in turn leading to an increase in the money supply. All else equal, this causes domestic interest rates to decrease and investors to invest in currencies with relatively higher interest rates, resulting in a decrease in the domestic currency's exchange value. (Choices A and B) Open market security purchases are indicative of an expansionary monetary policy, which would be used to increase GDP growth rates and put upward pressure on domestic inflation.
